lines.text: This is 99% Invisible.
lines.zh: 这里是《99% Invisible》。

lines.text: I'm Roman Mars.
lines.zh: 我是罗曼·马尔斯。

lines.text: Last August, producer Vivian Le received a voicemail that kicked off the first of several panic attacks that would span months.
lines.zh: 去年八月，制作人薇薇安·黎收到一条语音留言。从那时起，接下来的几个月里，她经历了好几次惊恐发作。

lines.text: Hi Vivian, this is Samir calling from Mercedes-Benz of Oakland.
lines.zh: 你好，薇薇安，我是奥克兰奔驰经销店的萨米尔。

lines.text: Please give me a call back when you get a chance.
lines.zh: 你有空时，请给我回个电话。

lines.text: Um, just something came up.
lines.zh: 嗯，是有这么个事。

lines.text: Someone submitted a lead under your name.
lines.zh: 有人用你的名字提交了购车意向。

lines.text: Just wanted to give you a quick call.
lines.zh: 我就想赶紧给你打个电话。

lines.text: The manager of a Mercedes-Benz dealership had called me to let me know that someone had walked into their dealership with a fake ID in my name and tried to drive out with a zero-down loan on a brand new Benz.
lines.zh: 这位奔驰经销店经理打电话告诉我，有人拿着写有我名字的假证件进了店，想办一笔零首付贷款，把一辆崭新的奔驰开走。

lines.text: My identity had been stolen.
lines.zh: 我的身份被人冒用了。

lines.text: That's the real Vivian Le.
lines.zh: 这位才是真正的薇薇安·黎。

lines.text: I mean, I've been working in the car business for a while, and I can tell when something's off.
lines.zh: 我在汽车这行干了有些年头了，一看就知道哪里不对劲。

lines.text: And the minute I saw the driver's license and information, nothing really matched up.
lines.zh: 我一看驾照和那些资料，就发现怎么都对不上。

lines.text: This is my man, Samir, the manager who tipped me off.
lines.zh: 这就是萨米尔，那位给我通风报信的经理。

lines.text: After I got that call, I found out that at some point, my personal information had been leaked in a data breach.
lines.zh: 接完那通电话，我才知道自己的个人信息早在某次数据泄露中就流出去了。

lines.text: Most likely, several people had been pretending to be me and using my social security number to attempt to get car loans, register for utilities, get car insurance, and rent multiple apartments and houses all under my name.
lines.zh: 很可能已经有好几个人冒充我，拿着我的社保号码，试着用我的名义申请车贷、开通水电、买车险，还租了好几套公寓和房子。

lines.text: When I see that, I feel for the people, because it's a pain to go and clean up all the mess that they create.
lines.zh: 遇到这种事，我挺替当事人难受的。别人捅了娄子，收拾起来可太折腾了。

lines.text: It was such a pain.
lines.zh: 真的太折腾了。

lines.text: Over the next several months, I needed to fill out multiple police reports, fill out FTC affidavits, assemble fraud packets, change every single password I've ever made in my entire life, and deal with debt collectors.
lines.zh: 接下来的几个月，我填了好几份警方报案材料和联邦贸易委员会的宣誓声明，整理了整套欺诈证明，把这辈子设过的密码全改了一遍，还得应付催债的人。

lines.text: And I had to go through each of these tedious, stress-inducing steps because this whole identity theft situation was impacting one very important thing: my credit score.
lines.zh: 这些又繁琐又让人焦虑的手续，我全都得一一办下来，因为身份被盗影响了一件特别重要的事：我的信用评分。

lines.text: And, like, you had stellar credit, so even if it's fraud, it still hurts your credit.
lines.zh: 你原本的信用那么好，可哪怕是别人冒用身份，也照样会伤到你的信用。

lines.text: It still does a bunch of stuff.
lines.zh: 还会惹出一大堆麻烦。

lines.text: A credit score is essentially a three-digit number that here in the U.S. usually ranges from 300 to 850.
lines.zh: 信用评分说白了就是个三位数，在美国通常介于 300 到 850 之间。

lines.text: It's a metric that lenders can use to predict your ability to pay back a loan.
lines.zh: 贷款机构用这个指标来判断你有没有能力还钱。

lines.text: The higher the number, the more likely you are to be approved for lines of credit.
lines.zh: 分数越高，获批信用额度的可能性就越大。

lines.text: Aside from applying for a new apartment every few years, I almost never questioned what my credit score was or where it came from.
lines.zh: 除了隔几年要申请租房，我几乎从来没想过自己的信用分有多少，也没有问过这分数从哪儿来。

lines.text: But in the months that followed, I found myself hyperfixated on that number and how to make it go back up because as I learned very quickly, those three little numbers are weirdly powerful.
lines.zh: 可在之后的几个月里，我满脑子都是这个分数，还有怎么把它提回去。我很快就发现，这小小的三位数，影响力大得出奇。

lines.text: If you have good credit, all they ask for is your name, date of birth, social security number, and address.
lines.zh: 只要信用好，对方要的就只有姓名、出生日期、社保号码和住址。

lines.text: If you have good credit, the system auto-approves you and you just buy a car and move on.
lines.zh: 信用好，系统就会自动批准，你买了车就可以走人。

lines.text: In the United States, your credit score decides where you can live, what car you can drive, and whether you can get a loan.
lines.zh: 在美国，信用分决定了你能住哪儿、能开什么车，以及能不能贷到款。

lines.text: And it's supposed to be objective, a precise, omniscient accounting of your financial health.
lines.zh: 按理说，这个分数应该是客观的，能准确又全面地反映你的财务状况。

lines.text: But as I started looking into it, I learned that the credit score is much less objective than it seems.
lines.zh: 可查下去我才发现，信用评分远没有看起来那么客观。

lines.text: What started as a simple tool for lenders ended up embedding itself in the lives of most Americans and feeding the same bias it claimed to solve.
lines.zh: 一开始，它只是放贷人手里一个简单的工具，后来却渗进了大多数美国人的生活，还助长了它原本声称要消除的偏见。

lines.text: Credit has existed for thousands of years in several forms.
lines.zh: 赊账和借贷的做法五花八门，几千年前就有了。

lines.text: But up until the early 19th century, basically the whole first chapter of American history, there were no credit scores because no one really needed them.
lines.zh: 可一直到十九世纪初，也就是美国历史最早的那一大段时期，根本没有信用评分，因为大家用不着它。

lines.text: Much of the credit that kept the economy moving was between businesses, like a wholesaler selling goods on credit to a shopkeeper.
lines.zh: 当时支撑经济运转的赊账，大多发生在商家之间，比如批发商先把货赊给店主。

lines.text: And in those early days, it was easy to know who to trust.
lines.zh: 在那个时候，要判断谁可信很容易。

lines.text: Communities were small, and chances are the wholesaler and the shopkeeper knew each other personally, or at least secondhand.
lines.zh: 社区都不大，批发商和店主十有八九认识，就算不认识，也能从熟人那里打听到。

lines.text: For many, many years, it's okay because they're repeat customers. The networks of credit are relatively limited.
lines.zh: 很长一段时间里，这套办法行得通，因为打交道的都是回头客，能赊账的圈子也就那么大。

lines.text: So you could write a letter to somebody you know in a nearby town and they could send a letter back and tell you whether they were trustworthy or not.
lines.zh: 你可以写信给邻镇的熟人，请对方回信，告诉你那个人信不信得过。

lines.text: This is Josh Lauer, professor of communication and author of Creditworthy: A History of Consumer Surveillance and Financial Identity in America.
lines.zh: 这位是传播学教授乔希·劳尔。他写过《谁值得信贷》，讲的是美国如何监控消费者，以及个人金融身份是怎么形成的。

lines.text: And he says that by the 1830s, that credit system built on trust was starting to erode.
lines.zh: 他说，到了十九世纪三十年代，这套靠熟人信任撑起来的信用体系开始瓦解。

lines.text: The country was getting bigger and more interconnected.
lines.zh: 国家越来越大，各地之间的往来也越来越多。

lines.text: Suddenly, a wholesaler in New York could be selling on credit to a shopkeeper from hundreds of miles away with no way to know if they could be trusted to pay back their debt.
lines.zh: 突然之间，纽约的批发商也可能要赊货给几百英里外的店主，却无从知道对方会不会还钱。

lines.text: The problem is that as societies get bigger, modern societies have more strangers, more opportunities to interact with people we don't know.
lines.zh: 社会越大，陌生人就越多，我们也越常跟不认识的人打交道。

lines.text: It becomes a problem because you can't identify people, you can't know that you can trust them or not trust them.
lines.zh: 这就成了个问题：你连对方是谁都弄不清，更不知道该不该信他。

lines.text: This was an era of industrialization.
lines.zh: 那是工业化的时代。

lines.text: Cities were growing rapidly and lenders in places like New York were interacting more and more with brand new borrowers they just didn't know.
lines.zh: 城市迅速扩大，纽约等地的放贷人越来越常遇到从未打过交道的借款人。

episodes.title: Know the Score
episodes.notes:
A credit score is essentially a three digit number that here in the US usually ranges from 300-850. It's a metric that lenders can use to predict your ability to pay back a loan. The higher the number, the more likely you are to be approved for lines of credit. In the United States, your credit score decides where you can live, what car you can drive and whether you can get a loan. It’s supposed to be objective—a precise, omniscient accounting of your financial health, but what started as a simple tool for lenders ended up embedding itself in the lives of most Americans, and feeding the same bias it claimed to solve.

episodes.title: 100 Objects #24: White House Solar Panels
episodes.notes:
In 1979, President Jimmy Carter took to the roof of the White House to announce the installation of 32 solar panels. In that speech, he outlined all the things that they could become: a curiosity, a museum piece, one of our nation's most potent and enduring symbols of a road not taken, or the start of a great adventure. They would become all but the last of those things…but why? Journalist and environmental activist Bill McKibben takes Roman Mars through the story of how a president showed the American people a powerful new technology promising abundant cheap energy and why Americans shrugged.

episodes.title: 100 Objects #23: Coin From the Ship of Gold
episodes.notes:
On August 20th, 1857 a ship set sail from the Port of San Francisco with 600 people and thousands of pounds of gold. That gold was destined for the vaults of New York City banks, but it never made it. Instead, the ship sank to the bottom of the ocean, taking all that gold with it. Executive Producer Annie Brown sits down with Roman Mars to tell the story of the sinking of the SS Central America and the gold that sparked the first global financial panic, helped fuel the Civil War, and—over a century later—ruined one man’s life.

episodes.title: The Ultraviolent, Wildly Successful, Uniquely American Phenomenon of Grand Theft Auto
episodes.notes:
Thursday, Nov. 19 will see the release of one of the biggest, most anticipated entertainment properties of the year: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

The first Grand Theft Auto game was released in 1997, and immediately stoked controversy with its aggressively satirical portrait of amoral, criminal American culture. Over the past 30 years, the franchise has continued to keep a sharp satirical eye on American society, and its often unpleasant excesses. The sixth installment promises to touch on hot-button issues like the war on drugs, police violence, conspiracy theories and influencer culture. And yet, even though the game has already made one billion dollars in pre-order sales, it might be the last time we ever see one of this scale.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Michael Barbaro talks with reporter Zachary Small, who covers video games for The Times, about Grand Theft Auto and how it became one of the biggest video game franchises of all time.

episodes.notes:
Era junio de 1997 cuando Celia Ramos comenzó a recibir las visitas de las enfermeras. Se presentaban en su casa, en una zona rural de Piura, Perú. Querían convencerla de que se sometiera a una operación para no volver a quedar embarazada: una ligadura de trompas. Y lo mismo hicieron con miles de mujeres, en distintas regiones, en lo que se convirtió en uno de los episodios más oscuros de Perú.

Join Noriko for an autumn walk in Liverpool as she shares recent reading discoveries, an unexpected conversation, and small ways to refresh her motivation.

She is enjoying an English translation of a Korean author’s science fiction short stories. Although she previously thought science fiction was not her genre, she finds the characters’ worries, values, and inner conflicts surprisingly familiar. Their journeys also prompt questions about space travel and moving to distant planets.

After visiting a Japanese-style bakery with her husband, Noriko had a brief conversation with a stranger in a car park lift. A woman noticed her bakery bag and asked what she had bought. This simple exchange left Noriko feeling happy and helped her reconsider the assumption that talking to strangers might be unwelcome. She reflects on her experiences in Japan, Belfast, and Liverpool, and considers trying a conversation herself when the circumstances feel right.

A recent modern dance performance exploring healthcare gave her a fresh perspective, while walking to energetic K-pop helps lift her mood. episodes.title: Season 3-169 人間関係は効率化できない？孤独と人とのつながりを考える
episodes.notes:
質問

今、人とつながっているなぁと感じていますか?

オンラインで知り合った人と、 本当の意味で深い関係を作ることはできると思いますか?

一人でいることと、孤独であることはどう違いますか?

Summary

今回のテーマは「孤独」と「人とのつながり」です。今はSNS、ビデオコール、Zoom、オンラインコミュニティなどを使って、世界中の人と簡単につながることができます。しかし、つながる方法が増えても、深い人間関係を感じられず、孤独を感じる人もいます。

コロナの後、仕事、勉強、買い物など、多くのことがオンラインでできるようになりました。生活はとても便利になりましたが、お店の人と話したり、近所の人と挨拶したり、知らない人と自然に話したりする小さな交流は減っているのかもしれません。

のりこさんはリバプールに引っ越してから、ブッククラブや哲学のディスカッションクラブなどに参加し、実際に人と会う交流を意識するようになりました。また、太宰治の『人間失格』を読んで、周りに人がたくさんいても、本当の自分を見せられなければ深い孤独を感じることがあると考えました。

一方で、オンラインでも深い関係を作ることはできると考えています。ただ、同じコミュニティに参加するだけでは十分ではありません。相手に興味を持つこと、話を聞くこと、何度も会うこと、コメントや返信をすることなど、小さな努力を続ける必要があります。

人間関係を作るためには時間がかかり、誤解されたり拒絶されたりする可能性もあります。それでも、自分から連絡したり、誘ったり、相手に歩み寄ったりすることが大切です。人間関係には効率化できない「面倒くささ」があり、その面倒くささこそが、人と深くつながるために必要なのではないか、ということを考えるエピソードです。

In this episode, Noriko explores loneliness and human connection in a world where technology makes it easier than ever to communicate. Social media, video calls, remote work, and online communities allow us to connect with people across the globe, yet many people still struggle with loneliness and a lack of meaningful relationships.

Reflecting on life after COVID, Noriko considers how convenience may have reduced some of the small, spontaneous interactions that once happened naturally in everyday life. She shares her experiences of joining a quiet book club and a philosophy discussion group in Liverpool, where in-person conversations have helped her build a stronger sense of local community.

She also connects the topic to Osamu Dazai’s No Longer Human, examining how someone can be surrounded by people while still experiencing profound loneliness when they cannot reveal their true self.

Finally, Noriko reflects on both online and offline relationships. Meaningful connection, she argues, requires time, curiosity, commitment, courage, and repeated effort. Human relationships cannot be completely optimized for convenience or efficiency. Sometimes, the inconvenient and difficult work of reaching out is exactly what allows deeper relationships to grow.

episodes.title: Season 3-168 芸術の秋：Frida Kahlo フリーダ・カーロと私のメキシコの思い出
episodes.notes:
質問：あなたにも、何年経っても心に残っていて、もう一度見たい作品や、もう一度訪れたい美術館がありますか？それはあなたの人生や思い出とどのようにつながっていますか？

Summary

今回のテーマは「芸術の秋」です。Norikoさんは夫とロンドンのTate Modernへ行き、大好きなメキシコの画家、Frida Kahloの特別展を見ました。

フリーダは1907年にメキシコシティで生まれました。子供の頃に病気になり、18歳のときには大きな交通事故に遭いました。もともとは医者になりたかったそうですが、事故によってその夢を続けることが難しくなりました。長い治療生活の中で絵を描き始め、自画像を通して体の痛み、孤独、愛、怒り、そして自分のアイデンティティを表現しました。

また、フリーダの人生では、画家ディエゴ・リベラとの複雑な関係も重要でした。二人は芸術や政治的な考え方を通して惹かれ合いましたが、離婚と再婚も経験しました。フリーダの伝統的で色鮮やかなメキシコの服装も、彼女を象徴するものになっています。

Norikoさんがフリーダを好きになった背景には、20代後半に一人でメキシコを旅行した経験があります。メキシコシティの「青い家」を訪れた思い出は今でも強く残っています。今回の展覧会は、フリーダの作品を見るだけではなく、若い頃の自分やメキシコでの思い出ともう一度つながる機会にもなりました。

In this episode of Japanese with Noriko, Noriko explores the idea of “autumn for the arts” through the life and work of Mexican painter Frida Kahlo. After visiting a special exhibition at Tate Modern in London with her husband, she reflects on Kahlo’s paintings, personal struggles, identity, and lasting influence.

Noriko introduces key moments from Kahlo’s life, including her childhood illness, the serious traffic accident she experienced at eighteen, and the long periods of treatment that followed. Originally interested in medicine, Kahlo began painting while spending extended periods in bed. Her self-portraits became a powerful way to express physical pain, loneliness, love, anger, and questions about identity. Noriko also discusses Kahlo’s complicated relationship with Mexican muralist Diego Rivera and her iconic traditional Mexican fashion.

The exhibition also brings back Noriko’s memories of traveling alone through Mexico in her twenties. She recalls the vivid colors of Mexican cities and her visit to Kahlo’s famous Blue House in Mexico City. Through art, travel, and memory, this Japanese podcast episode explores how meaningful places and artworks can stay with us for many years.

Japanese summary

今回は、いつもの本の紹介とは少し違い、のりこさんが本好きのYukoさんに読書についていろいろな質問をしました。

Yukoさんは、ストーリーのある本や情報が入った新書をよく読みます。本を選ぶときは、最初の1ページや1行目を読んで、そのときのフィーリングを大切にしているそうです。しかし最近は、信頼している人から直接おすすめされた本なら、中身をあまり確認しなくても買うことがあると話しました。人からすすめられた本は、その人と一緒に話したいという気持ちもあり、最後まで読みやすくなるそうです。

読書をするお気に入りの場所は、お風呂と階段です。特にお風呂ではタオルを使いながら本を読みます。また、本にメモをするときにはフリクションペンを使い、コーヒーやお茶を飲みながら読むこともあります。

本は図書館で借りるより書店で買うことが多く、本屋さんに行くと店内を一通り歩くのも好きです。また、友達と本を貸し合う楽しさや、中身を隠して本を渡す方法についても話しました。

買った本をすぐ読むこともあれば、「積読」してしまうこともあります。そして、Yukoさんが読書を好きになったきっかけは、学生時代に教科書で吉本ばななさんの『TUGUMI』の一部を読んだことでした。

最後には、Yukoさんが『ノルウェイの森』に再チャレンジしていること、のりこさんが村上春樹さんの旅行エッセイ『遠い太鼓』を読み終えたことについて話しました。二人にとって、本は一人で読むだけではなく、人とつながり、会話を楽しむきっかけにもなっています。

本好きの人に聞いてみよう

- 普段、どんなジャンルの本をよく読んでいますか。- 本を選ぶとき、何を基準にしていますか。- 最初の1ページや1行目を読んでから、買うかどうか決めていますか。- 本の表紙やデザイン、装丁を見て、内容を知らずに思わず買ったことはありますか。- 「この本はやめておこう」と思うのは、どんなときですか。- 本を読むお気に入りの場所はありますか。- 読書をするときの決まった習慣や、お供にしているものはありますか。- 本は書店で買うことが多いですか。それとも図書館で借りることが多いですか。- 図書館に定期的に通っていますか。- 必ず立ち寄る書店はありますか。- 買った本をすぐに読む派ですか。それとも積読する派ですか。- 読書が好きになったきっかけは何ですか。- 今読んでいる本や最近読んだ本を、一冊紹介してもらえますか。

episodes.title: The history of light (classic)
episodes.notes:
How do you measure human progress? Light is the answer.

For thousands of years, getting light was a huge hassle. You had to make candles from scratch. This is not as romantic as it sounds. You had to get a cow, raise the cow, feed the cow, kill the cow, get the fat out of the cow, cook the fat, dip wicks into the fat. All that — for not very much light. Now, if we want to light a whole room, we just flip a switch.

Nobel-winning economist Bill Nordhaus passed away last week. He was known for his work on the economics of climate change, but he also came up with this idea that the history of light explains reveals why the world today is the way it is. It explains why we aren't all subsistence farmers, and why we can afford to have artists and massage therapists and plumbers. (And, yes, people who make podcasts about the history of light.) The history of light is the history of economic growth — of things getting faster, cheaper, and more efficient. It shows us the pie can get bigger, sometimes, there can be a type of progress where everyone is better off.

On today's show, one of our all time favorites: How we got from dim little candles made out of cow fat, to as much light as we want at the flick of a switch, and how that is a measure of what economic progress means.

episodes.title: More Perfect: Cruel and Unusual
episodes.notes:
This week, we’re replaying the inaugural episode of More Perfect (first aired in 2016) we explore three little words embedded in the 8th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution: “cruel and unusual.” America has long wrestled with this concept in the context of our strongest punishment, the death penalty. A majority of “we the people” (61 percent, to be exact) are in favor of having it, but inside the Supreme Court, opinions have evolved over time in surprising ways.

And outside of the court, the debate drove one woman in the UK to take on the U.S. death penalty system from Europe. It also caused states to resuscitate old methods used for executing prisoners on death row. And perhaps more than anything, it forced a conversation on what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.

In this episode, we also include a new conversation with Harvard law professor Carol Steiker and former death-row inmate Damien Nichols about the moment the death penalty finds itself in now. After the botched execution of Christa Pike, and with the government considering livestreaming a firing squad execution, how do we understand the death penalty in 2026?

How can they navigate the divides in a party that now stretches from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Adam Hamilton in Kansas? How do they prevent all their new voters in this election from flipping back in the next one? Can they turn this victory into a springboard to an even bigger and more durable Democratic majority in 2028 and beyond?

We will have two episodes that try to answer these questions from different angles, one from the center of the party and one from the left. First, representing the more center view, we have Adam Jentleson, the founder and president of the Searchlight Institute, a Washington think tank. Jentleson is a veteran of the Senate; he served as deputy chief of staff to the former Senate majority leader Harry Reid and chief of staff to Senator John Fetterman. He’s also the author of two books, “Kill Switch: The Rise of the Modern Senate and the Crippling of American Democracy,” and “Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power,” which came out in September.

Note: An earlier version of this episode misstated the religious denomination of Adam Hamilton. He is a United Methodist minister, not an Episcopal minister.

episodes.title: How the Democrats Did It
episodes.notes:
President Trump is primarily responsible for the Republican shellacking on Tuesday. But to get over the finish line in so many places — across the Midwest and deep into the South – Democrats had to run the right candidates, and those candidates ran very different campaigns.

So how exactly did those Democrats do it? Michelle Goldberg, my colleague at New York Times Opinion, did amazing work this past year covering the biggest races — traveling to Texas, Michigan, Maine and other states, meeting with the candidates, and getting a sense of their campaigns on the ground. She joins me for a deep dive into the most exciting — and shocking — wins, and what they reveal about the new Democratic Party that will emerge out of this election.

chat.followUpQuestion: Why did lenders need a new way to judge trust?

replies.result:
A dealership voicemail tipped producer Vivian Le off to identity theft ({t:3}). As she worked to repair her credit, she learned how much a three-digit score can shape where you live, what you drive, and whether you can borrow ({t:29}).

The episode traces how lending moved from personal trust ({t:37}) to credit scoring, and asks why a tool meant to reduce bias can still reinforce it.

When wholesalers and shopkeepers knew each other, they could extend credit on reputation or ask a mutual contact ({t:37}). By the 1830s, businesses were lending to people hundreds of miles away. A wholesaler needed a way to judge whether a stranger would pay them back ({t:43}).

A credit score helps lenders estimate whether a borrower will repay a loan ({t:23}). Vivian shows how that same number became a gatekeeper for decisions beyond lending, including where people can live ({t:29}).
Vivian traces the attempted car purchase back to a data breach ({t:14}). She found that people had also been using her identity to apply for loans, utilities, insurance, and rentals ({t:15}).

chat.fallback: The episode starts with Vivian Le discovering that someone tried to buy a car under her name ({t:8}). Her experience leads into a look at how credit scores came to govern everyday decisions ({t:29}).
